questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Reflection of light; spherical mirrors and mirror formula
questions.question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image formed, and what is its nature?
options: 60 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted
12 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted
60 cm behind the mirror, virtual and erect
12 cm behind the mirror, virtual and erect

solution.key_concept: Mirror formula $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ with the Cartesian sign convention.
steps: For the concave mirror, $u = -30$ cm and $f = -20$ cm.
So $v = -60$ cm. The negative sign means the image is in front of the mirror, so it is real and inverted.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): 60 cm in front of the mirror, real and inverted
solution.why_not_others: A distance of 12 cm comes from adding the reciprocals wrongly. An image behind the mirror would need the object to lie between F and P, but here the object lies beyond F.
solution.common_trap: Writing $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{f} + \frac{1}{u}$, which gives 12 cm.
solution.time_saving_tip: The object lies between F and C, so the real image must form beyond C (beyond 40 cm).

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Reflection of light; spherical mirrors and mirror formula
questions.question: An object 6 cm tall is placed 30 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. What are the size, nature and position of the image?
options: 2 cm, inverted, real, 10 cm in front of the mirror
6 cm, erect, virtual, 30 cm behind the mirror
2 cm, erect, virtual, 10 cm behind the mirror
6 cm, inverted, real, 30 cm in front of the mirror

solution.key_concept: A convex mirror ($f > 0$) always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image.
steps: Take $u = -30$ cm and $f = +15$ cm.
$\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{30} = \frac{1}{10}$, so $v = +10$ cm, which is behind the mirror.
Image height $= 6 \times \frac{1}{3} = 2$ cm, and the image is erect and virtual.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): 2 cm, erect, virtual, 10 cm behind the mirror
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) has the wrong sign of m and v. Option (2) comes from taking u as positive. Option (4) comes from treating the convex mirror's f as negative.
solution.common_trap: Using $f = -15$ cm for a convex mirror.
solution.time_saving_tip: A convex mirror can never give a real or magnified image, so options (1), (2) and (4) can be rejected at once.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Reflection of light; spherical mirrors and mirror formula
questions.question: A concave mirror of focal length 15 cm forms a real image that is three times the size of the object. What is the distance of the object from the mirror?

solution.key_concept: A real image has negative magnification, $m = -\frac{v}{u}$.
steps: For a real image, $m = -3$, so $v = 3u$.
This gives $u = -20$ cm, so the object is 20 cm from the mirror.
solution.why_not_others: 10 cm would give a virtual image with $m = +3$. 30 cm is the centre of curvature, where $m = -1$. 60 cm is the image distance, not the object distance.
solution.common_trap: Taking $m = +3$, which gives the virtual-image answer of 10 cm.
solution.time_saving_tip: A real magnified image needs the object between F and C, that is, between 15 cm and 30 cm. Only 20 cm lies in this range.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Reflection of light; spherical mirrors and mirror formula
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A concave mirror of radius of curvature 40 cm has a focal length of magnitude 20 cm both in air and when immersed in water.
statements.R: The focal length of a spherical mirror depends on the refractive index of the surrounding medium.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: For a mirror, $f = R/2$, which depends only on geometry.
steps: $f = R/2 = 20$ cm whatever the medium, so A is true.
Reflection does not involve the refractive index, so the focal length of a mirror is independent of the medium. R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R is false, so options (1), (2) and (4) are ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Confusing mirrors with lenses, whose focal length does change with the surrounding medium.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Reflection of light; spherical mirrors and mirror formula
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: An object placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 20 cm forms its image at infinity.
statements.II: If a plane mirror is rotated through $15^\circ$ while the incident ray is kept fixed, the reflected ray turns through $15^\circ$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: A convex mirror always forms a virtual image within its focal length. Rotating a mirror by $\theta$ turns the reflected ray by $2\theta$.
steps: Statement I: $u = -20$ cm and $f = +20$ cm, so $\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{20}$, giving $v = +10$ cm. The image is not at infinity, so I is incorrect.
Statement II: the reflected ray turns through $2 \times 15^\circ = 30^\circ$, so II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are false, so every option that calls either one correct is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Applying the concave-mirror rule (object at F gives image at infinity) to a convex mirror, and forgetting the factor of 2 for a rotating mirror.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refraction at plane and spherical surfaces
questions.question: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters glass of refractive index 1.5. What are its wavelength and frequency inside the glass?
options: 400 nm; frequency reduced by a factor of 1.5
600 nm; frequency reduced by a factor of 1.5

solution.key_concept: Frequency does not change on refraction, while $\lambda_{medium} = \lambda/n$.
steps: $\lambda_{glass} = 600/1.5 = 400$ nm.
The frequency is set by the source, so it stays the same.
solution.why_not_others: 900 nm comes from multiplying by n. Options (3) and (4) wrongly let the frequency change.
solution.common_trap: Thinking the frequency falls when the light slows down.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refraction at plane and spherical surfaces
questions.question: A tank contains a 9 cm layer of a liquid of refractive index 1.5, with a 12 cm layer of water (refractive index $4/3$) floating on top of it. What is the apparent depth of the bottom of the tank when viewed from air near the normal?

solution.key_concept: For layered media seen from outside, apparent depth $= \sum t_i/n_i$.
steps: Water layer: $12/(4/3) = 9$ cm.
Liquid layer: $9/1.5 = 6$ cm.
Total apparent depth $= 9 + 6 = 15$ cm.
solution.why_not_others: 6 cm is the shift, not the apparent depth. 21 cm is the real depth. 29.5 cm comes from multiplying each thickness by n.
solution.common_trap: Multiplying by the refractive index instead of dividing.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refraction at plane and spherical surfaces
questions.question: A convex spherical surface of radius of curvature 10 cm separates air (object side) from glass of refractive index 1.5. A point object in air lies on the axis 40 cm from the surface. How far from the surface, inside the glass, is the image formed?

solution.key_concept: Refraction at a single spherical surface: $\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$.
solution.why_not_others: 20 cm comes from a sign error in the u term. 40 cm comes from dropping $n_2$. 30 cm comes from ignoring the object term, which treats the object as being at infinity.
solution.common_trap: Taking u as positive for a real object.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refraction at plane and spherical surfaces
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Normal shift produced by a glass slab of thickness 9 cm and refractive index 1.5 (observer in air)

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Apparent depth of a coin under 8 cm of water ($n = 4/3$), viewed from air near the normal

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Apparent height above the surface of a bird 12 cm above water, as seen by a fish just below the surface ($n_{water} = 4/3$)

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Apparent depth of the bottom of 4 cm of water ($n = 4/3$) resting on 6 cm of glass ($n = 1.5$), viewed from air

solution.key_concept: Apparent depth $= h_{real}/n_{rel}$, with $n_{rel}$ = (index of object medium)/(index of observer medium). The normal shift of a slab is $t(1 - 1/n)$.
steps: A: $9(1 - 2/3) = 3$ cm, so A matches III.
B: $8/(4/3) = 6$ cm, so B matches I.
C: $n_{rel} = 1/(4/3) = 3/4$, so the apparent height is $12/(3/4) = 16$ cm. C matches II.
solution.why_not_others: Every other option mismatches at least one pair. For example, option (1) confuses the slab shift (3 cm) with the apparent depth of the coin (6 cm).
solution.common_trap: For the fish, multiplying by $3/4$ gives 9 cm. Objects viewed from a denser medium actually appear farther away.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refraction at plane and spherical surfaces
questions.question: Which of the following statements about refraction are correct?

statements.A: When light passes from vacuum into a medium of refractive index n, both its speed and its wavelength decrease by a factor of n.
statements.B: The normal shift produced by a glass slab depends on the distance of the object from the slab.
statements.C: A glass slab with parallel faces produces a lateral displacement of a ray but no deviation.
statements.D: A fish looking up from under water sees an object above the surface as farther away than it really is.
statements.E: In the relation $\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$, R is positive when the centre of curvature lies on the incident-light side.

solution.key_concept: These statements test basic refraction facts, the slab shift and the sign convention for spherical surfaces.
steps: A is true: $v = c/n$ and $\lambda_{medium} = \lambda/n$.
B is false: the shift $t(1 - 1/n)$ does not depend on object position.
C is true: emergent rays are parallel to incident rays.
D is true: viewing from a denser into a rarer medium makes objects appear farther away.
E is false: R is positive when the centre lies on the refracted-light side.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) leaves out D. Option (2) includes the false B. Option (4) includes the false E and leaves out A.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a slab's shift changes with object distance.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Thin lens formula and lens maker formula
questions.question: An equiconvex lens is made of glass of refractive index 1.5, and each surface has a radius of curvature of 20 cm. What is the power of the lens in air?

solution.key_concept: For an equiconvex lens, $f = R/[2(n-1)]$, and $P = 1/f$ with f in metres.
solution.why_not_others: +0.05 D comes from using f in cm. -5 D has the wrong sign for a convex lens. +2.5 D comes from using the plano-convex formula.
solution.common_trap: Using f in centimetres when calculating power.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Thin lens formula and lens maker formula
questions.question: An object is placed 10 cm from a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. What are the position of the image and the magnification?
options: 30 cm on the other side of the lens, magnification $-3$
6 cm on the same side as the object, magnification $+0.6$
30 cm on the same side as the object, magnification $+3$
30 cm on the same side as the object, magnification $-3$

solution.key_concept: Thin lens formula $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$, with $m = v/u$.
steps: Take $u = -10$ cm and $f = +15$ cm.
$\frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{15} - \frac{1}{10} = -\frac{1}{30}$, so $v = -30$ cm, on the same side as the object.
$m = v/u = (-30)/(-10) = +3$. The image is virtual, erect and magnified.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): 30 cm on the same side as the object, magnification $+3$
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) has the wrong sign of v. Option (2) comes from using the mirror formula. Option (4) uses the mirror magnification $-v/u$.
solution.common_trap: Using $1/v + 1/u = 1/f$ or $m = -v/u$ for a lens.
solution.time_saving_tip: An object inside the focal length of a convex lens always gives a virtual, erect, magnified image.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Thin lens formula and lens maker formula
questions.question: A thin convex lens made of glass of refractive index 1.5 has a focal length of 20 cm in air. What is its focal length when it is completely immersed in water of refractive index $4/3$?

solution.key_concept: From the lens maker's formula, $f_{liquid}/f_{air} = (n_g - 1)/(n_g/n_l - 1)$.
steps: $f_{water} = 4 \times 20 = 80$ cm, and it is still converging because $n_g > n_l$.
solution.why_not_others: 26.7 cm comes from simply multiplying by $n_l$. 40 cm is a wrong ratio. -80 cm reverses the sign, which happens only when the liquid is denser than the glass.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the lens becomes diverging in any liquid.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Thin lens formula and lens maker formula
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A convex lens made of glass of refractive index 1.5 behaves as a diverging lens when immersed in a liquid of refractive index 1.6.
statements.R: For a given lens, the focal length for violet light is shorter than that for red light.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: When $n_{21} < 1$, the sign of f reverses. Chromatic dispersion makes f depend on wavelength.
steps: Here $n_{21} = 1.5/1.6 < 1$, so $(n_{21} - 1)$ is negative and f becomes negative. A is true.
Violet light has a larger n, so its f is shorter. R is true.
R deals with wavelength dependence, not with the effect of the medium, so it does not explain A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: R does not explain the sign reversal, which ruins option (1). Both statements are true, which rules out options (3) and (4).
solution.common_trap: Choosing option (1) just because both statements are about lenses.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Thin lens formula and lens maker formula
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: A plano-convex lens of refractive index 1.5 with a curved surface of radius 15 cm has a focal length of 30 cm in air.
statements.II: When an equiconvex lens of focal length 20 cm is cut into two halves by a plane perpendicular to its principal axis, each half has a focal length of 10 cm.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: For a plano-convex lens, $f = R/(n-1)$. Cutting a lens perpendicular to the axis doubles f for each half.
steps: Statement I: $f = 15/0.5 = 30$ cm, so I is correct.
Statement II: each half is plano-convex, so $f = 2 \times 20 = 40$ cm, not 10 cm. II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: II halves f instead of doubling it, so options (1) and (4) are wrong. I is correct, so option (2) is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that halving the lens halves its focal length.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Total internal reflection and its applications
questions.question: What is the critical angle for light going from a medium of refractive index 2 into air?

solution.key_concept: The critical angle is given by $\sin i_c = n_{rarer}/n_{denser}$.
steps: $i_c = 30^\circ$.
solution.why_not_others: $60^\circ$ comes from using cosine instead of sine. $45^\circ$ corresponds to $n = \sqrt{2}$. $15^\circ$ has no basis.
solution.common_trap: Writing $\cos i_c = 1/n$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Total internal reflection and its applications
questions.question: A point source of light is placed 8 cm below the surface of a liquid of refractive index $5/3$. What is the radius of the circle on the surface through which light emerges into air?

solution.key_concept: The radius of the circle of emergence is $r = \frac{h}{\sqrt{n^2 - 1}}$.
solution.why_not_others: 10.7 cm comes from multiplying h by $4/3$. 4.8 cm is $h/n$. 13.3 cm is $hn$.
solution.common_trap: Inverting the factor $\sqrt{n^2 - 1}$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Here $\sin i_c = 3/5$, so $\tan i_c = 3/4$ and $r = h \tan i_c = 6$ cm.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Total internal reflection and its applications
questions.question: A right-angled isosceles glass prism is to be used in a periscope to turn light through $90^\circ$ by total internal reflection. Light falls on the hypotenuse face at $45^\circ$. Which of the following refractive indices of the prism material would make this possible?

solution.key_concept: TIR at $45^\circ$ requires $i_c < 45^\circ$, which means $n > \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$.
steps: The condition is $\sin i_c = 1/n < \sin 45^\circ = 1/\sqrt{2}$.
So $n > 1.414$. Only 1.50 satisfies this.
solution.why_not_others: 1.33, 1.20 and 1.40 are all below $\sqrt{2}$. With these, $i_c > 45^\circ$ and light would escape by refraction.
solution.common_trap: Picking 1.40 because it looks close enough to $\sqrt{2}$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Total internal reflection and its applications
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Brilliant sparkle of a diamond

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Optical fibre

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Mirage in a desert

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Totally reflecting prism in a periscope

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Core has a higher refractive index than the cladding

list_II.label: IV
list_II.text: Total internal reflection at rarer layers of hot air near the ground

solution.key_concept: Each application relies on a different feature of total internal reflection.
steps: Diamond sparkles because its critical angle is small, about $24.4^\circ$, so A matches III.
An optical fibre needs a core of higher index than the cladding, so B matches I.
A mirage is TIR at the rarer, hot air near the ground, so C matches IV.
A periscope uses a $45^\circ$ prism with $n > \sqrt{2}$, so D matches II.
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) swaps diamond and fibre. Option (3) swaps fibre and prism. Option (4) swaps mirage and prism.
solution.common_trap: Linking the high refractive index of diamond with optical fibres.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Total internal reflection and its applications
questions.question: Which of the following statements about total internal reflection are correct?

statements.A: Total internal reflection can occur only when light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium.
statements.B: In a given glass, violet light has a smaller critical angle than red light.
statements.C: During total internal reflection, a small part of the light is always refracted into the rarer medium.
statements.D: The critical angle at a glass-water interface is smaller than at a glass-air interface.
statements.E: Optical fibres are used in endoscopy.

solution.key_concept: The critical angle is given by $\sin i_c = n_{rarer}/n_{denser}$, and TIR involves no loss.
steps: A is true: this is the first condition for TIR.
B is true: violet light has a larger n, so its $i_c$ is smaller.
C is false: in TIR all the light is reflected with no loss.
D is false: water has a higher index than air, so $\sin i_c$ is larger and $i_c$ is larger.
E is true: endoscopy is a stated application of optical fibres.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and E only
solution.why_not_others: Options (2) and (4) include the false D. Option (3) includes the false C.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that a denser surrounding medium lowers the critical angle.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Magnification and power of a lens
questions.question: A concave lens has a focal length of magnitude 25 cm. What is its power?

solution.key_concept: Power $P = 1/f$ with f in metres. A diverging (concave) lens has negative power.
steps: For a concave lens, $f = -25$ cm $= -0.25$ m.
solution.why_not_others: $+4$ D has the wrong sign for a diverging lens. $-0.04$ D comes from using f in cm. $+0.25$ D is just f in metres, not its reciprocal, and it also has the wrong sign.
solution.common_trap: Taking f in cm or forgetting the negative sign of a concave lens.
solution.time_saving_tip: 100 divided by f in cm gives P in dioptre directly: $100/25 = 4$, and the concave lens makes it negative.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Magnification and power of a lens
questions.question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. What are the linear magnification and the nature of the image?

solution.key_concept: For a lens, $m = f/(f+u)$. A negative m means the image is real and inverted.
steps: Take $u = -30$ cm and $f = +20$ cm.
Since m is negative, the image is real and inverted, and twice the size of the object.
solution.why_not_others: $+2$ comes from a sign error; a virtual image needs the object within f. $-0.5$ inverts the ratio. $-1.5$ comes from taking $u/f$.
solution.common_trap: Using the mirror relation $m = -v/u$ for a lens, which flips the sign.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Magnification and power of a lens
questions.question: A thin convex glass lens ($n = 1.5$) has a power of $+5$ D in air. What is its power when it is completely immersed in water of refractive index $4/3$?

solution.key_concept: By the lens maker's formula, $1/f \propto (n_{21} - 1)$, where $n_{21} = n_{lens}/n_{medium}$.
steps: The power scales by $(1/8)/(1/2) = 1/4$, so $P_{water} = 5/4 = +1.25$ D (f becomes 80 cm).
solution.why_not_others: $+5$ D assumes the power does not change with the medium. $-1.25$ D wrongly reverses the sign; that happens only if the liquid is denser than the glass. $+20$ D multiplies by 4 instead of dividing.
solution.common_trap: Treating the focal length of a lens as independent of the surrounding medium.
solution.time_saving_tip: Take the ratio of $(n_{21} - 1)$ values directly instead of finding the radii.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Magnification and power of a lens
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image of a real object.
statements.R: The power of a diverging lens is negative.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Image nature for a concave lens; sign convention for lens power.
steps: For a real object, a concave lens always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image, so A is true.
Diverging lenses have negative power, so R is true.
The sign of the power is a convention. It does not explain why the image is always virtual and diminished, so R does not explain A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are true, so options (3) and (4) fail. R is a sign convention and does not explain the nature of the image, so option (1) fails.
solution.common_trap: Picking option (1) just because both statements concern a concave lens.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Magnification and power of a lens
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: A single thin lens forms a real image of a small square object placed perpendicular to its axis with linear magnification of magnitude 3. The image is inverted and its area is 9 times that of the object.
statements.II: An object placed 15 cm from a convex lens of power $+5$ D forms a virtual, erect image with magnification $+2$.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: A real image from a single lens has $m < 0$. Areal magnification is $m^2$. Also, $m = f/(f+u)$.
steps: Statement I: a real image means $m = -3$, so the image is inverted. Its area ratio is $m^2 = 9$. Statement I is correct.
Statement II: $f = 1/5$ m $= 20$ cm and $u = -15$ cm.
$m = \frac{20}{20 - 15} = +4$, not $+2$. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement II gives the wrong magnification, which rules out options (1) and (4). Statement I is correct, which rules out options (2) and (4).
solution.common_trap: Taking the areal magnification as 3 instead of $m^2$, or accepting $+2$ without calculating.
solution.time_saving_tip: Use $m = f/(f+u)$ directly instead of finding v first.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Combination of thin lenses in contact
questions.question: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm is placed in contact with a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. What is the equivalent focal length of the combination?

solution.key_concept: For thin lenses in contact, $1/F = 1/f_1 + 1/f_2$, with signs.
steps: $F = +20$ cm, so the combination is converging.
solution.why_not_others: $+6.67$ cm ignores the negative sign of the concave lens. $-10$ cm adds the focal lengths directly. $-20$ cm has the wrong sign.
solution.common_trap: Adding focal lengths instead of their reciprocals.
solution.time_saving_tip: Add powers: $+10$ D $- 5$ D $= +5$ D, so $F = 20$ cm.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Combination of thin lenses in contact
questions.question: Two thin convex lenses of focal lengths 20 cm and 30 cm are placed coaxially, 10 cm apart, in air. What is the equivalent focal length of the system?

solution.key_concept: For separated lenses, $\frac{1}{F} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} - \frac{d}{f_1 f_2}$.
solution.why_not_others: 12 cm treats the lenses as being in contact. 10 cm adds the d term instead of subtracting it. 50 cm simply adds the focal lengths.
solution.common_trap: Treating separated lenses as if they were in contact.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Combination of thin lenses in contact
questions.question: An equiconvex lens of power $+5$ D has one of its faces silvered. The silvered curved face acts as a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. What is the focal length of the resulting system, which behaves as a concave mirror?

solution.key_concept: For a silvered lens, $P = 2P_{lens} + P_{mirror}$. Light passes through the lens twice.
solution.why_not_others: 6.67 cm counts the lens power only once (15 D). 4 cm doubles the mirror power instead of the lens power (25 D). 10 cm is just the mirror alone.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting that light passes through the lens twice.
solution.time_saving_tip: Work in dioptres and convert to cm only at the end.

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Concave lenses of focal lengths 25 cm and 100 cm in contact

solution.key_concept: For lenses in contact, $P = P_1 + P_2$, with $P = 1/f$ in metres and the correct signs.
steps: A: $+2 - 2 = 0$ D, so the pair acts like a plane glass plate (III).
solution.why_not_others: The other matchings either swap B and C or assign the wrong sign to the diverging pair.
solution.common_trap: Using f in cm or dropping the negative sign of concave lenses.
solution.time_saving_tip: Convert each focal length to dioptres as $100/f_{cm}$, then add.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Combination of thin lenses in contact
questions.question: Which of the following statements about combinations of thin lenses are correct?

statements.A: The powers of thin lenses in contact add algebraically.
statements.B: The total magnification of a combination of lenses equals the sum of the individual magnifications.
statements.C: A lens of power $+5$ D in contact with a lens of power $-5$ D behaves like a plane glass plate.
statements.D: For two separated lenses, if the image formed by the first lens lies beyond the second lens, it acts as a virtual object for the second lens with positive u.
statements.E: Two convex lenses, each of focal length 20 cm, placed 40 cm apart have an equivalent focal length of 10 cm.

options: A, C, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Powers add for lenses in contact, magnifications multiply, and separated lenses use the d term.
steps: A is true: $P = P_1 + P_2$.
B is false: $m = m_1 m_2$, a product, not a sum.
C is true: the net power is zero.
D is true, as stated in the stepwise method for separated lenses.
E is false: $1/F = 1/20 + 1/20 - 40/400 = 0$, so F is infinite, not 10 cm.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A, C and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) misses the true statement D. Option (2) includes the false statement B. Option (4) includes the false statement E.
solution.common_trap: Treating the lenses in E as if in contact, which gives 10 cm.
solution.time_saving_tip: When $d = f_1 + f_2$ for two convex lenses, the system is afocal.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refraction of light through a prism
questions.question: A thin prism of refracting angle $5^\circ$ is made of glass of refractive index 1.6. What is the deviation it produces?

solution.key_concept: For a thin prism, $\delta = (n-1)A$.
steps: $\delta = (1.6 - 1) \times 5^\circ = 0.6 \times 5^\circ = 3^\circ$.
solution.why_not_others: $8^\circ$ uses $nA$. $13^\circ$ uses $(n+1)A$. $5^\circ$ is just the prism angle.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting to subtract 1 from n.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refraction of light through a prism
questions.question: A prism of refracting angle $60^\circ$ has a refractive index of $\sqrt{2}$. What is its angle of minimum deviation?

solution.key_concept: $n = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin(A/2)}$.
steps: $\sqrt{2} = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{60^\circ + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin 30^\circ}$, so $\sin\left(\frac{60^\circ + \delta_m}{2}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
$\frac{60^\circ + \delta_m}{2} = 45^\circ$, so $\delta_m = 30^\circ$.
solution.why_not_others: $45^\circ$ is the angle of incidence at minimum deviation. $60^\circ$ is the prism angle. $15^\circ$ comes from halving $\delta_m$.
solution.common_trap: Reporting $(A + \delta_m)/2$, which is i, as the deviation.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refraction of light through a prism
questions.question: A thin prism of angle $6^\circ$ has refractive indices 1.56 for violet light and 1.52 for red light. What is the angular dispersion it produces?

solution.key_concept: Angular dispersion $= (n_v - n_r)A$.
steps: Angular dispersion $= 0.04 \times 6^\circ = 0.24^\circ$.
solution.why_not_others: $3.24^\circ$ is the mean deviation $(n_y - 1)A$ with $n_y = 1.54$. $0.074$ is the dispersive power, which is dimensionless and not an angle. $0.04^\circ$ forgets to multiply by A.
solution.common_trap: Confusing angular dispersion with dispersive power or with mean deviation.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refraction of light through a prism
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: For a thin prism, the deviation increases steadily as the angle of incidence is increased.
statements.R: For a thin prism, the deviation is given by $\delta = (n-1)A$.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: For a thin prism, the deviation $(n-1)A$ is independent of i.
steps: R is the standard thin-prism result, so R is true.
Since $\delta = (n-1)A$ does not depend on i, the deviation does not increase with i. A is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A is false but R is true
solution.why_not_others: A is false, so options (1), (2) and (3) are ruled out.
solution.common_trap: Applying the U-shaped i-versus-$\delta$ behaviour of a general prism to a thin prism.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Refraction of light through a prism
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: When light passes through an equilateral prism at minimum deviation, the angle of refraction at the first face is $60^\circ$.
statements.II: No ray can emerge from the second face of a prism of refracting angle $85^\circ$ made of glass whose critical angle is $40^\circ$, whatever the angle of incidence.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: At minimum deviation, $r = A/2$. No emergence is possible if $A > 2i_c$.
steps: Statement I: $r_1 = A/2 = 30^\circ$, not $60^\circ$. Statement I is incorrect.
Statement II: $2i_c = 80^\circ$ and $A = 85^\circ > 80^\circ$, so no ray can emerge. Statement II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
solution.why_not_others: Statement I confuses r with A, which rules out options (1) and (3). Statement II satisfies the no-emergence condition, which rules out option (2).
solution.common_trap: Taking r = A instead of A/2 at minimum deviation.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Microscope and astronomical telescope and their magnifying powers
questions.question: A simple microscope uses a convex lens of focal length 5 cm. What is its magnifying power when the final image is formed at the near point ($D = 25$ cm)?

solution.key_concept: For a simple microscope with the image at the near point, $m = 1 + D/f$.
solution.why_not_others: 5 is the value for an image at infinity ($D/f$). 4 subtracts 1 instead of adding it. 0.2 is $f/D$.
solution.common_trap: Using $D/f$ when the image is at the near point.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Microscope and astronomical telescope and their magnifying powers
questions.question: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 2 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm, with a tube length of 20 cm. What is its magnifying power when the final image is at infinity ($D = 25$ cm)?

solution.key_concept: For a compound microscope in normal adjustment, $m = \frac{L}{f_o}\cdot\frac{D}{f_e}$.
solution.why_not_others: 60 uses $1 + D/f_e$, which applies to an image at the near point. 10 counts only the objective. 5 counts only the eyepiece.
solution.common_trap: Mixing the near-point and infinity formulas for the eyepiece.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Microscope and astronomical telescope and their magnifying powers
questions.question: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 50 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. What is its magnifying power when the final image is formed at the near point ($D = 25$ cm)?

solution.key_concept: For a telescope with the image at the near point, $m = \frac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \frac{f_e}{D}\right)$.
solution.why_not_others: 10 is the value for normal adjustment. 8 uses $(1 - f_e/D)$. 60 uses $(1 + D/f_e)$, which is the microscope eyepiece factor.
solution.common_trap: Using the microscope factor $D/f_e$ instead of $f_e/D$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Microscope and astronomical telescope and their magnifying powers
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Simple microscope, image at near point

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Simple microscope, image at infinity

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Astronomical telescope, normal adjustment

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Compound microscope, normal adjustment

solution.key_concept: Standard magnifying-power formulas for optical instruments.
steps: A: $1 + D/f$ (III).
C: $f_o/f_e$ (IV).
solution.why_not_others: The other options swap the near-point and infinity cases of the simple microscope, or swap the telescope and compound microscope formulas.
solution.common_trap: Associating $1 + D/f$ with an image at infinity.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Microscope and astronomical telescope and their magnifying powers
questions.question: Which of the following statements about microscopes and telescopes are correct?

statements.A: In a compound microscope, both $f_o$ and $f_e$ are small, with $f_o < f_e$.
statements.B: The objective of an astronomical telescope has a large focal length and a large aperture.
statements.C: The final image formed by an astronomical telescope is erect.
statements.E: Using an eyepiece of larger focal length increases the magnifying power of a telescope in normal adjustment.

options: A, B, C and D only

solution.key_concept: Design features and image characteristics of optical instruments.
steps: A is true, as stated for a compound microscope.
B is true: a large aperture improves light-gathering and resolution.
C is false: the final image is inverted.
D is true: mirrors do not produce chromatic aberration.
E is false: since $m = f_o/f_e$, a larger $f_e$ decreases m.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) includes the false statement C. Option (3) includes the false statement E and omits A. Option (4) omits the true statement B.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the telescope image is erect, or that a larger eyepiece focal length means more magnification.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Wavefront and Huygens' principle
questions.question: A narrow illuminated slit acts as a line source of light. The shape of the wavefront emerging from it is:

solution.key_concept: The shape of a wavefront depends on the geometry of the source.
steps: A point source gives spherical wavefronts.
A line source gives cylindrical wavefronts.
A source at infinity gives plane wavefronts.
A narrow slit is a line source, so its wavefront is cylindrical.
solution.why_not_others: Spherical wavefronts come from a point source. Plane wavefronts come from a very distant source. Elliptical wavefronts are not associated with any of these sources.
solution.common_trap: Assuming that every source produces spherical wavefronts.
solution.time_saving_tip: Remember the sequence point, line, infinity: spherical, cylindrical, plane.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Wavefront and Huygens' principle
questions.question: The intensity of a cylindrical wavefront from a line source is $I$ at a distance of 2 m from the source. Neglecting absorption, what is the intensity at a distance of 8 m?

solution.key_concept: For cylindrical waves, intensity varies as $1/r$.
steps: Use $I \propto 1/r$ for a cylindrical wave.
Therefore $I' = I/4$.
solution.why_not_others: $I/16$ applies the $1/r^2$ law, which holds only for spherical waves. $I/2$ uses a $1/\sqrt{r}$ dependence. $4I$ inverts the ratio.
solution.common_trap: Applying the inverse-square law to a line source.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Wavefront and Huygens' principle
questions.question: A plane wavefront travels in glass of refractive index 1.5. According to Huygens' principle, what is the radius of a secondary wavelet $2 \times 10^{-9}$ s after it starts from a point on the wavefront? (Speed of light in vacuum $= 3 \times 10^8$ m/s)

solution.key_concept: Secondary wavelets spread with the speed of light in the medium in which they travel.
steps: The speed in glass is $v = c/n = 3\times10^8/1.5 = 2\times10^8$ m/s.
The radius is $r = vt = 2\times10^8 \times 2\times10^{-9} = 0.4$ m.
So $r = 40$ cm.
solution.why_not_others: 60 cm uses the speed in vacuum. 90 cm multiplies $c$ by $n$. 20 cm takes half the distance travelled, confusing radius with diameter.
solution.common_trap: Using the speed of light in vacuum for wavelets inside a medium.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Wavefront and Huygens' principle
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: Light from a very distant star reaching the earth can be treated as a beam of parallel rays.
statements.R: Rays of light are always parallel to the wavefront.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: Rays are normal to wavefronts, and a distant source produces plane wavefronts.
steps: A source at a very large distance produces plane wavefronts.
Rays are normal to a plane wavefront, so all of them are parallel to one another. A is true.
Rays are perpendicular to the wavefront, not parallel to it. R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R is false, so any option that treats R as true is wrong. A is correct because a distant source gives plane wavefronts.
solution.common_trap: Confusing 'rays parallel to each other' with 'rays parallel to the wavefront'.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Wavefront and Huygens' principle
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In Huygens' construction, the new wavefront is the forward envelope of the secondary wavelets, which spread with the speed of the wave in that medium; the backward wavelets are ignored.
statements.II: If the distance from the source is doubled, the intensity of a spherical wave falls to one-fourth, whereas that of a cylindrical wave falls to one-half.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Huygens' principle, and the variation of intensity with distance for different wavefronts.
steps: Statement I restates Huygens' construction: the forward envelope gives the new wavefront, the wavelets move with the wave speed in that medium, and backward wavelets are ignored. It is correct.
For a spherical wave, $I \propto 1/r^2$, so doubling $r$ gives $I/4$.
For a cylindrical wave, $I \propto 1/r$, so doubling $r$ gives $I/2$.
Statement II is therefore correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both statements agree exactly with the principle and with the intensity laws, so no option that marks either one incorrect can be right.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that the backward wavelets also form a wavefront, or using $1/r^2$ for every type of wave.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Laws of reflection and refraction using Huygens' principle
questions.question: When a light wave passes from air into glass, which of the following remains unchanged?
options: Direction of propagation for oblique incidence

solution.key_concept: Frequency is fixed by the source and does not change across a boundary.
steps: Speed decreases in glass.
Wavelength changes in proportion to speed.
Frequency stays the same.
solution.why_not_others: Speed and wavelength both decrease in glass. For oblique incidence the ray bends towards the normal, so its direction changes.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that wavelength stays constant while frequency changes.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Laws of reflection and refraction using Huygens' principle
questions.question: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters a medium of refractive index 1.5. What is its wavelength in the medium? (Take the refractive index of air as 1.)

solution.key_concept: $\lambda_2 = \lambda_1 n_1/n_2$, since frequency is unchanged.
steps: $\lambda_2 = 600 \times 1/1.5$.
$\lambda_2 = 400$ nm.
solution.why_not_others: 900 nm multiplies by $n$ instead of dividing. 600 nm assumes the wavelength does not change. 267 nm divides by $n^2$.
solution.common_trap: Assuming wavelength is unchanged in the way frequency is.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Laws of reflection and refraction using Huygens' principle
questions.question: In Huygens' construction for refraction, a plane wavefront meets a plane boundary at an angle of incidence of $60^\circ$. The speed of light in the first medium is $\sqrt{3}$ times its speed in the second medium. What is the angle of refraction?

solution.key_concept: $\sin i/\sin r = v_1/v_2$
steps: $\sin r = \sin 60^\circ \times v_2/v_1 = (\sqrt{3}/2)(1/\sqrt{3})$.
solution.why_not_others: $60^\circ$ ignores the change in speed. $90^\circ$ wrongly treats this as the critical-angle case. $45^\circ$ results from an error in the ratio.
solution.common_trap: Inverting the ratio to $v_2/v_1$ in Snell's law. This gives $\sin r > 1$, which is impossible.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Laws of reflection and refraction using Huygens' principle
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Ratio $\sin i/\sin r$ obtained from Huygens' construction

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Wavelength of light in the second medium

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Quantity unchanged when light crosses a boundary

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Speed of light in a denser medium as predicted by the corpuscular theory

list_II.label: IV
list_II.text: Greater than in the rarer medium

solution.key_concept: Snell's law from wave theory, and how the wavelength and frequency of light behave at a boundary.
steps: A: $\sin i/\sin r = v_1/v_2$, so A-III.
B: $\lambda_2 = \lambda_1 n_1/n_2$, so B-II.
C: frequency is unchanged, so C-I.
D: Newton's corpuscular theory wrongly predicted a larger speed in a denser medium, so D-IV.
solution.why_not_others: The other matchings swap the Snell ratio with the wavelength expression, or confuse frequency with the corpuscular prediction.
solution.common_trap: Believing that the corpuscular theory predicted a smaller speed in a denser medium.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Laws of reflection and refraction using Huygens' principle
questions.question: Which of the following statements about reflection and refraction explained by Huygens' principle are correct?

statements.A: Light bends towards the normal when it slows down on entering a medium.
statements.B: In reflection, the incident and reflected wavelets travel equal distances in equal times, which leads to $i = r$.
statements.C: The ratio $\sin i/\sin r$ is equal to $n_1/n_2$.
statements.D: Reflection changes the wavelength of light but not its frequency.
statements.E: Huygens' construction can also explain total internal reflection and the critical angle.

solution.key_concept: Laws of reflection and refraction derived from the propagation of secondary wavelets.
steps: A is true: a lower speed in the second medium makes the ray bend towards the normal.
B is true: equal speeds in the same medium give congruent triangles, so $i = r$.
C is false: $\sin i/\sin r = n_2/n_1$.
D is false: reflection changes neither the speed, the frequency nor the wavelength.
E is true: Huygens' construction also explains TIR and the critical angle.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): A, B and E only
solution.why_not_others: The options containing C or D include a false statement. 'A and B only' leaves out the true statement E.
solution.common_trap: Inverting the ratio of refractive indices in Snell's law.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Interference; Young's double-slit experiment and fringe width
questions.question: In Young's double-slit experiment, light of wavelength 500 nm is used. The slit separation is 0.5 mm and the screen is 1 m away. What is the fringe width?

solution.key_concept: $\beta = \lambda D/d$
steps: $\beta = 1\times10^{-3}$ m $= 1$ mm.
solution.why_not_others: 0.5 mm and 2 mm come from mixing up $d$ in the formula. 10 mm comes from a power-of-ten error in unit conversion.
solution.common_trap: Errors in converting nm and mm to metres.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Interference; Young's double-slit experiment and fringe width
questions.question: The fringe width in a Young's double-slit experiment performed in air is 0.6 mm. The whole apparatus is then immersed in water of refractive index $4/3$. What is the new fringe width?

solution.key_concept: In a medium the wavelength becomes $\lambda/n$, so $\beta' = \beta/n$.
solution.why_not_others: 0.8 mm multiplies by $n$. 0.6 mm ignores the medium. 0.34 mm divides by $n^2$.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that immersion increases the fringe width.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Interference; Young's double-slit experiment and fringe width
questions.question: In Young's double-slit experiment, the slit separation is 1 mm and the screen is 1 m away. One slit is covered with a thin transparent film of thickness 10 $\mu$m and refractive index 1.5. What is the shift of the fringe pattern, and in which direction?
options: 5 mm away from the covered slit

solution.key_concept: Fringe shift $= (\mu - 1)tD/d$, towards the covered slit.
steps: Shift $= (1.5 - 1) \times 10\times10^{-6} \times 1/(1\times10^{-3})$.
Shift $= 5\times10^{-3}$ m $= 5$ mm.
The extra optical path makes the pattern shift towards the covered slit.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): 5 mm towards the covered slit
solution.why_not_others: 'Away' gives the wrong direction. 15 mm uses $\mu$ in place of $(\mu - 1)$. 10 mm leaves out the refractive-index factor completely.
solution.common_trap: Using $\mu t$ instead of $(\mu - 1)t$, or getting the direction of the shift wrong.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Interference; Young's double-slit experiment and fringe width
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: In Young's double-slit experiment, covering one slit with a thin transparent film does not change the fringe width.
statements.R: The film shifts the entire fringe pattern away from the covered slit.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: A film over one slit shifts the pattern but does not change $\beta = \lambda D/d$.
steps: $\lambda$, $D$ and $d$ are unchanged, so $\beta$ is unchanged. A is true.
The pattern shifts by $(\mu - 1)tD/d$ towards the covered slit, not away from it. R is false.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): A is true but R is false
solution.why_not_others: R states the wrong direction of shift, so any option that treats R as true is wrong.
solution.common_trap: Believing that the film changes the fringe width, or that the pattern shifts away from the covered slit.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Interference; Young's double-slit experiment and fringe width
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: In Young's double-slit experiment with two identical slits, the intensity at a point where the path difference is $\lambda/3$ is one-fourth of the maximum intensity.
statements.II: If the intensities of two coherent interfering waves are in the ratio 9 : 1, the ratio of maximum to minimum intensity is 4 : 1.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: $I = 4I_0\cos^2(\phi/2)$ and $I_{max}/I_{min} = ((\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2})/(\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2}))^2$
steps: Statement I: $\phi = (2\pi/\lambda)(\lambda/3) = 2\pi/3$.
$I = 4I_0\cos^2(\pi/3) = 4I_0 \times 1/4 = I_0 = I_{max}/4$, so I is correct.
Statement II: $\sqrt{I_1}:\sqrt{I_2} = 3:1$.
$I_{max}/I_{min} = (4/2)^2 = 4$, so II is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
solution.why_not_others: Both calculations confirm the statements, so no option that marks either one incorrect can be right.
solution.common_trap: Using $\cos^2\phi$ instead of $\cos^2(\phi/2)$, or using the intensity ratio directly without taking square roots.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Coherent sources and sustained interference
questions.question: Two sources of light are said to be coherent if they have:
options: The same frequency and a constant phase difference
The same amplitude but different frequencies
The same intensity, whatever their phase relation
The same frequency and a randomly varying phase difference

solution.key_concept: Coherence requires the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
steps: A constant phase difference keeps the interference pattern stationary.
This requires the same frequency together with a fixed phase relation.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): The same frequency and a constant phase difference
solution.why_not_others: Different frequencies or a randomly varying phase destroy coherence. Equal intensity alone does not make sources coherent.
solution.common_trap: Equating coherence with equal amplitude or equal intensity.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Coherent sources and sustained interference
questions.question: Two independent sodium lamps produce intensities $I$ and $4I$ at a point on a screen. What is the resultant intensity observed at that point?

solution.key_concept: Intensities from incoherent sources simply add.
steps: Independent lamps are incoherent.
solution.why_not_others: $9I$ and $I$ are the coherent maximum $(\sqrt{I}+\sqrt{4I})^2$ and minimum $(\sqrt{4I}-\sqrt{I})^2$. $3I$ is the difference of the intensities.
solution.common_trap: Applying the coherent superposition formula to independent sources.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Coherent sources and sustained interference
questions.question: Two coherent sources, each of intensity $I_0$, superpose at a point with a phase difference of $\pi/3$. What is the resultant intensity at that point?

solution.why_not_others: $4I_0$ is the maximum, at $\phi = 0$. $2I_0$ is the incoherent sum. $I_0$ uses $\cos^2\phi$ instead of $\cos^2(\phi/2)$.
solution.common_trap: Forgetting to halve the phase difference.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Coherent sources and sustained interference
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Young's double-slit arrangement

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Colours of a thin oil film

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Two independent sodium lamps

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Laser

list_II.label: I
list_II.text: Coherent sources by division of amplitude

list_II.label: II
list_II.text: Coherent sources by division of wavefront

solution.key_concept: Methods of producing coherent sources, and the distinction between coherent and incoherent sources.
steps: YDSE divides the wavefront, so A-II.
Thin films divide the amplitude, so B-I.
Independent lamps are incoherent and their intensities add, so C-III.
A laser is highly coherent, so D-IV.
solution.why_not_others: The other matchings swap division of wavefront with division of amplitude, or treat lamps as coherent.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up division of wavefront (YDSE) with division of amplitude (thin films).

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Coherent sources and sustained interference
questions.question: Which of the following statements about sustained interference are correct?

statements.A: The two sources must be coherent.
statements.B: Waves of equal amplitude give zero minimum intensity and hence the best contrast.
statements.C: A Fresnel biprism produces coherent sources by division of amplitude.
statements.D: The phase of light from an ordinary bulb changes roughly every $10^{-10}$ s, so two such bulbs cannot produce an observable interference pattern.
statements.E: Wide slits placed far apart give the most clearly resolved fringes.

solution.key_concept: Conditions for sustained, well-contrasted interference.
steps: A is true: coherence is essential.
B is true: equal amplitudes give $I_{min} = 0$.
C is false: a biprism divides the wavefront, not the amplitude.
D is true: rapid random phase changes make the pattern shift too fast to observe.
E is false: the slits should be narrow and closely spaced so that the fringes are wide.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: The options containing C or E include a false statement. 'A and B only' leaves out the true statement D.
solution.common_trap: Classifying the Fresnel biprism as a division-of-amplitude device.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Diffraction due to a single slit; width of central maximum
questions.question: Monochromatic light of wavelength $600\ \text{nm}$ falls normally on a single slit of width $0.2\ \text{mm}$. What is the linear width of the central maximum on a screen placed $1\ \text{m}$ from the slit?

solution.key_concept: The linear width of the central maximum is $W = 2\lambda D/a$.
steps: $W = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{a} = \dfrac{2 \times 600\times10^{-9} \times 1}{0.2\times10^{-3}}$
$W = 6\times10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 6\ \text{mm}$
solution.why_not_others: 3 mm comes from using $\lambda D/a$, which is only the half-width. 12 mm comes from wrongly using $4\lambda D/a$. 0.6 mm is a powers-of-ten slip.
solution.common_trap: Taking the central maximum width as $\lambda D/a$ instead of $2\lambda D/a$.
solution.time_saving_tip: Compute $\lambda D/a$ first (3 mm), then double it.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Diffraction due to a single slit; width of central maximum
questions.question: In air, a single-slit set-up gives a central maximum of linear width $4.0\ \text{mm}$ on a screen. The entire apparatus is then immersed in a liquid of refractive index $4/3$, with the slit and screen positions unchanged. What is the new width of the central maximum?

solution.key_concept: In a liquid of refractive index $n$, the wavelength becomes $\lambda/n$. Since $W \propto \lambda$, the width also falls by a factor of $n$.
solution.why_not_others: 5.33 mm comes from multiplying by $n$ instead of dividing. 4.0 mm assumes the medium has no effect. 1.5 mm comes from halving and then dividing by $n$.
solution.common_trap: Thinking the pattern spreads out in a denser medium. In fact the wavelength decreases, so the central maximum narrows.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Diffraction due to a single slit; width of central maximum
questions.question: Light of wavelength $600\ \text{nm}$ falls normally on a single slit. The second minimum of the diffraction pattern is observed at an angle of $30^\circ$ from the central direction. What is the width of the slit?

solution.key_concept: The minima of single-slit diffraction satisfy $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$.
steps: For the second minimum, $n = 2$.
$a = \dfrac{2\lambda}{\sin 30^\circ} = \dfrac{2\times 600\ \text{nm}}{0.5} = 2400\ \text{nm}$
$a = 2.4\ \mu\text{m}$
solution.why_not_others: 1.2 μm uses $n = 1$. 3.0 μm uses the secondary-maximum condition $(n+\frac{1}{2})\lambda$ with $n = 2$. 0.6 μm comes from multiplying by $\sin 30^\circ$ instead of dividing.
solution.common_trap: Mixing up the minimum condition $a\sin\theta = n\lambda$ with the approximate secondary-maximum condition $a\sin\theta = (n+\frac{1}{2})\lambda$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Diffraction due to a single slit; width of central maximum
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: In single-slit diffraction, the central maximum becomes wider when the slit is made narrower.
statements.R: The intensity of the secondary maxima decreases rapidly as their order increases.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: The width of the central maximum is $2\lambda D/a$, so it varies inversely with the slit width $a$.
steps: A is true: $W = 2\lambda D/a$ increases as $a$ decreases.
R is true: the secondary maxima fall off rapidly in intensity.
R describes intensity, not width. It therefore does not explain why the central maximum widens.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are factually correct, so options (3) and (4) are ruled out. Option (1) fails because R gives no reason for the width depending on $a$.
solution.common_trap: Picking option (1) just because both statements are about the diffraction pattern.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Diffraction due to a single slit; width of central maximum
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: For a slit of width $1\ \text{mm}$ illuminated by light of wavelength $500\ \text{nm}$, the Fresnel distance is $2\ \text{m}$.
statements.II: If the slit width and the wavelength are both doubled, the Fresnel distance remains unchanged.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: The Fresnel distance is $z_F = a^2/\lambda$.
steps: Statement I: $z_F = \dfrac{(10^{-3})^2}{5\times10^{-7}} = 2\ \text{m}$. It is correct.
Statement II: the new distance is $\dfrac{(2a)^2}{2\lambda} = 2\,\dfrac{a^2}{\lambda}$.
So the Fresnel distance doubles, and Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (3): Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I checks out numerically, and Statement II ignores the square on $a$. So options (1), (2) and (4) are wrong.
solution.common_trap: Treating $z_F$ as proportional to $a/\lambda$ rather than $a^2/\lambda$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Polarization, plane-polarized light and Brewster's law
questions.question: Unpolarized light falls on the surface of a transparent medium of refractive index $\sqrt{3}$. At what angle of incidence will the reflected light be completely plane-polarized?

solution.key_concept: Brewster's law states $\tan i_B = n$.
steps: $\tan i_B = \sqrt{3}$
$i_B = 60^\circ$
solution.why_not_others: $30^\circ$ is the refraction angle at the Brewster angle, or the result of using $\cot i_B = n$. $45^\circ$ corresponds to $n = 1$. $90^\circ$ is grazing incidence.
solution.common_trap: Using $\sin i_B = 1/n$, which is the critical-angle relation, instead of $\tan i_B = n$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Polarization, plane-polarized light and Brewster's law
questions.question: Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ passes through two ideal polaroids whose pass axes are inclined at $30^\circ$ to each other. What is the intensity of the light emerging from the second polaroid?

solution.key_concept: The first polaroid transmits $I_0/2$. Malus' law then applies to the second polaroid.
steps: After the first polaroid: $I_1 = I_0/2$.
After the second: $I = I_1\cos^2 30^\circ = \dfrac{I_0}{2}\times\dfrac{3}{4}$
solution.why_not_others: $3I_0/4$ applies Malus' law directly to the unpolarized light. $I_0/8$ uses $\sin^2 30^\circ$ in place of $\cos^2 30^\circ$. $I_0/2$ ignores the second polaroid.
solution.common_trap: Applying $\cos^2\theta$ to unpolarized light without first halving the intensity.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Polarization, plane-polarized light and Brewster's law
questions.question: A ray of unpolarized light strikes a transparent slab at the Brewster angle. The angle of refraction inside the slab is $37^\circ$. What is the refractive index of the slab? (Take $\tan 53^\circ = 4/3$.)

solution.key_concept: At the Brewster angle, $i_B + r = 90^\circ$ and $\tan i_B = n$.
steps: $i_B = 90^\circ - 37^\circ = 53^\circ$
$n = \tan 53^\circ = 4/3$
solution.why_not_others: $3/4$ is $\tan 37^\circ$, taking the refraction angle as $i_B$. $3/5$ is $\sin 37^\circ$. $5/3$ is $1/\sin 37^\circ$, which wrongly uses the critical-angle relation.
solution.common_trap: Substituting the refraction angle directly into $\tan i_B = n$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Polarization, plane-polarized light and Brewster's law
questions.question: Match List-I with List-II and choose the correct answer.

list_I.label: A
list_I.text: Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ through one ideal polaroid

list_I.label: B
list_I.text: Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ through two crossed polaroids

list_I.label: C
list_I.text: Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ through two polaroids with pass axes at $45^\circ$

list_I.label: D
list_I.text: Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ through two crossed polaroids with a third placed between them at $45^\circ$

solution.key_concept: The first polaroid transmits $I_0/2$. Each later polaroid multiplies the intensity by $\cos^2\theta$.
steps: A: one polaroid gives $I_0/2$, so A matches III.
B: crossed polaroids give $\frac{I_0}{2}\cos^2 90^\circ = 0$, so B matches II.
C: $\frac{I_0}{2}\cos^2 45^\circ = I_0/4$, so C matches IV.
D: $\frac{I_0}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = I_0/8$, so D matches I.
solution.why_not_others: Option (1) swaps C and D. Option (2) applies Malus' law to unpolarized light in A and C. Option (3) assigns $I_0/8$ to crossed polaroids, ignoring that they transmit zero.
solution.common_trap: Thinking that inserting a third polaroid between crossed polaroids cannot let any light through.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Polarization, plane-polarized light and Brewster's law
questions.question: Which of the following statements about polarization are correct?

statements.A: Sound waves in air cannot be polarized.
statements.B: At the Brewster angle, the reflected light is completely plane-polarized, with vibrations perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
statements.C: For glass of refractive index 1.5, the Brewster angle is about $33.7^\circ$.
statements.D: Sunlight scattered at $90^\circ$ to the incident direction is plane-polarized.
statements.E: Rotating a single polaroid in a beam of unpolarized light changes the transmitted intensity.

options: A, B, D and E only

solution.key_concept: Only transverse waves can be polarized. Brewster's law is $\tan i_B = n$. One polaroid transmits $I_0/2$ whatever its orientation.
steps: A is true: sound in air is longitudinal.
B is true: this is the standard Brewster-angle result.
C is false: $\tan^{-1}(1.5) \approx 56.3^\circ$, while $33.7^\circ$ is the refraction angle.
D is true: scattering polarizes light, and light scattered at $90^\circ$ is plane-polarized.
E is false: the intensity stays at $I_0/2$ for every orientation.
solution.final_answer: Option (1): A, B and D only
solution.why_not_others: Option (2) includes the false statement C. Options (3) and (4) include the false statement E, and option (3) also leaves out the true statement A.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the Brewster angle with the corresponding refraction angle, $90^\circ - i_B$.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Uses of plane-polarized light and Polaroid
questions.question: Polaroid sunglasses are effective in reducing glare from a wet road mainly because the light reflected from the road is
options: of shorter wavelength than the incident light
diffracted strongly by the road surface

solution.key_concept: Light reflected from horizontal surfaces is partly plane-polarized horizontally.
steps: Reflection from a horizontal surface partly polarizes the light horizontally.
The Polaroid lenses block this horizontal component, which cuts the glare.
solution.why_not_others: If the reflected light were unpolarized, a Polaroid would only halve it and would not remove glare selectively. Reflection does not change the wavelength. Diffraction plays no role in glare.
solution.common_trap: Thinking sunglasses work simply by darkening, without using polarization.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Uses of plane-polarized light and Polaroid
questions.question: A Polaroid sheet consists of long-chain molecules aligned in one direction. The light transmitted by the sheet has its electric vector
options: parallel to the direction of the molecular chains
along the direction of propagation of light
vibrating in all directions perpendicular to propagation
perpendicular to the direction of the molecular chains

solution.key_concept: The aligned chains absorb the electric-field component parallel to them and transmit the perpendicular component.
steps: The component of E parallel to the chains is absorbed.
The component perpendicular to the chains passes through, so the pass axis is perpendicular to the chains.
solution.final_answer: Option (4): perpendicular to the direction of the molecular chains
solution.why_not_others: The parallel component is the one absorbed, not transmitted. Light is transverse, so E never lies along the direction of propagation. Vibration in all perpendicular directions describes unpolarized light.
solution.common_trap: Assuming the pass axis lies along the chains.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Uses of plane-polarized light and Polaroid
questions.question: An adjustable train window is made of two ideal Polaroid sheets. Unpolarized sunlight of intensity $800\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ falls on it, and the transmitted intensity is $100\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. What is the angle between the pass axes of the two sheets?

solution.key_concept: The first sheet transmits $I_0/2$. The second sheet then follows Malus' law.
steps: After the first sheet: $800/2 = 400\ \text{W m}^{-2}$.
$400\cos^2\theta = 100$, so $\cos^2\theta = 1/4$.
$\cos\theta = 1/2$, giving $\theta = 60^\circ$.
solution.why_not_others: $30^\circ$ comes from using $\sin^2\theta$ instead of $\cos^2\theta$. $45^\circ$ would transmit $200\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. $90^\circ$ would transmit nothing.
solution.common_trap: Writing $800\cos^2\theta = 100$ without first halving the unpolarized intensity.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Uses of plane-polarized light and Polaroid
questions.question: Given below are two statements: Assertion A and Reason R. Choose the correct answer.

statements.A: 3D movies use two oppositely polarized images that are viewed through polarizing glasses.
statements.R: Polarized light is used in photoelasticity to reveal stress patterns in transparent models.

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

solution.key_concept: 3D movies and photoelasticity are two separate applications of polarized light.
steps: A is true: each eye receives only one of the two oppositely polarized images.
R is true: photoelasticity reveals stress in transparent models.
R describes an unrelated application, so it does not explain A.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
solution.why_not_others: Both statements are correct, which rules out options (3) and (4). There is no causal link between them, which rules out option (1).
solution.common_trap: Choosing option (1) because both statements involve polarized light.

questions.subject: physics
questions.topic: Uses of plane-polarized light and Polaroid
questions.question: Given below are two statements. Choose the most appropriate answer.

statements.I: When a single Polaroid is rotated in a beam of unpolarized light, the transmitted intensity varies between a maximum and zero.
statements.II: Polaroid sunglasses cut glare from roads because light reflected from horizontal surfaces is partly polarized vertically.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

solution.key_concept: Unpolarized light through one Polaroid gives a constant $I_0/2$. Light reflected from horizontal surfaces is partly polarized horizontally.
steps: Statement I: the intensity stays at $I_0/2$ for every orientation. It varies only when the incident light is already polarized. Statement I is incorrect.
Statement II: reflected glare is partly polarized horizontally, not vertically. Statement II is incorrect.
solution.final_answer: Option (2): Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
solution.why_not_others: Statement I describes what happens with polarized incident light, not unpolarized light. Statement II has the wrong direction of polarization. Since both are false, options (1), (3) and (4) fail.
solution.common_trap: Confusing the behaviour of a rotating analyser in polarized light with that of a single Polaroid in unpolarized light.
